## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

In the model of AI compute investment developed here, capacity, timing, and the training-inference split answer to different forces. Optimal capacity is pinned down by the revenue and cost technology and is invariant to beliefs about when AGI arrives (Proposition 1); the entry trigger is compressed by the threat of preemption (Proposition 3); and the training fraction is governed by beliefs about the arrival rate $\lambda$ (Proposition 1). That separation is what makes belief errors asymmetric: a firm with the wrong timeline installs the same capacity, and carries the same coupon, as a firm with the right one, so the whole cost of the error runs through the entry trigger and the training allocation.

Three core tensions drive the results.

First, *current cash flow versus future capability*: firms balance inference revenue in regime $L$, which funds operations and services debt, against training undertaken in regime $L$ whose payoff arrives only as capability in regime $H$. The optimal training fraction $\phi^*$ increases in the arrival rate $\lambda$, so more optimistic firms allocate more to training, a prediction qualitatively consistent with the differences in reported training allocation across the archetypes in @sec-calibration.

Second, *growth-option upside versus leverage and default risk*: the *faith-based survival* channel holds at the calibrated optimum but not throughout the parameter space. Its $A_{\text{eff}}$-channel threshold, $\underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$, lies well below the optimal $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, so at baseline a larger training allocation lowers the default boundary rather than raising it (Proposition 2); the channel reverses for beliefs below $\lambda \approx 0.034$, where the optimal allocation is too inference-heavy for the continuation-value gain to offset the sacrificed cash flow. A levered firm therefore faces a two-sided trade-off with an interior optimum: it must invest early enough to preempt its rival and train enough to sustain the option value of regime $H$, without entering so close to its default boundary that it fails if the regime switch does not arrive.

Third, *the asymmetric cost of belief mismatches*: preemption compresses the value of waiting, which makes timing errors costly. Numerical Finding 1 shows that in the calibration this cost is asymmetric. Conservative underinvestment is costlier in expected value than aggressive overinvestment for the same magnitude of belief error, because under-allocating to training forfeits the option value of regime $H$ that dominates firm value. Overinvestment, by contrast, carries substantially higher tail risk: an aggressive firm enters at a lower trigger while over-training depresses the regime-$L$ revenue that services its debt, leaving it much closer to its default boundary at entry. Capacity is not the channel: optimal capacity is independent of beliefs (Proposition 1), so the coupon burden is the same for every belief type. Within the model, this asymmetry bears on the *extreme* end of the observed capital commitments rather than on aggressive investment generally. Moderate overinvestment is cheap: about 6\% of unlevered value at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.20$ when the true rate is $\lambda = 0.10$, compared with roughly 23\% at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.50$ (@fig-investment-dilemma). At the extreme end the five-year default probability at $\ell = 0.40$ also rises to 5.04\%, nearly eight times the baseline. Both value-loss percentages are those of the reduced model, computed under the pure-power discounting convention used to price the option; re-solving the exact piecewise stopping problem preserves the ranking but moves the magnitudes materially, raising the conservative loss to about 40\% and lowering the aggressive loss to about 0.5\% (Internet Appendix B). Commitments at that end of the range are therefore more readily reconciled with genuinely optimistic beliefs than with a low-cost posture, though the model contains no exercise that separates beliefs from signaling or agency motives, and the comparison rests on a stylized calibration: it is illustrative rather than a formal identification result.

The model abstracts from several dimensions of the decision executives face: talent constraints, safety and alignment objectives, geopolitical competition, entrants such as DeepSeek [@deepseek2025r1], and the debate over whether pre-training scaling has reached its limits.^[Reuters, "OpenAI and others seek new path to smarter AI as current methods hit limitations," November 11, 2024.] The training fraction is fixed at investment time, whereas dynamic reallocation and inference-time scaling create a richer optimization. The model is also silent on the \$600 billion revenue gap between AI infrastructure spending and current AI revenue [@cahn2024gap], which may discipline the investment race through financial markets before any technological resolution occurs.

Three extensions follow directly: dynamic learning about $\lambda$ from capability milestones, dynamic training-inference reallocation with $\phi$ responding to realized demand, and financial frictions such as credit constraints, dynamic leverage adjustment, and debt renegotiation. The most natural empirical companion is a *formal* revealed-beliefs methodology that inverts the model to recover implied AI timeline beliefs from observable investment decisions; the illustrative inversions in @sec-calibration and @sec-valuation demonstrate the concept but fall short of estimation, which would require additional instruments, proper treatment of the uncertainty in the calibration parameters (particularly $\sigma$ and $\alpha$), and a richer model with dynamic $\phi$ and heterogeneous information.
